winterreise.title: Winterreise
winterreise.overview: Twenty-four songs to poems by Wilhelm Müller, written in 1827, the year before Schubert died. A young man leaves the town where the girl he loved has chosen someone richer, and walks out into the winter. There is no plot beyond that walk: frozen rivers, a weather vane, a lime tree, crows, a signpost, a graveyard that will not take him in. Each song is a station of the journey and of his mind, and the cycle ends, without consolation, with an old organ-grinder in the snow.

muellerin.title: Die schöne Müllerin
muellerin.overview: Twenty songs to poems by Wilhelm Müller, written in 1823. A young miller sets out on his travels, follows a brook to a mill and falls in love with the miller's daughter. For a while she seems to return his love; then a huntsman in green arrives and she turns to him. The brook is his companion from the first song to the last, when he lies down in it and the brook sings him to sleep.

schwanengesang.title: Schwanengesang
schwanengesang.overview: Not a cycle Schubert planned but the songs of his last months, 1828, gathered after his death by his publisher Tobias Haslinger and given the title 'Swan Song'. Seven are to poems by Ludwig Rellstab, six to Heinrich Heine, and the last, Die Taubenpost, to Johann Gabriel Seidl.

dichterliebe.title: Dichterliebe
dichterliebe.overview: Sixteen songs to poems from Heinrich Heine's Lyrisches Intermezzo, written in a few days in late May 1840, Schumann's 'year of song', the year he was finally allowed to marry Clara Wieck. A poet falls in love in May, is rejected, and goes through bitterness, irony, dreams and tears, until he buries his love and his songs in a giant coffin and sinks it in the sea. The piano often has the last and most tender word.

liederkreis39.title: Liederkreis, Op. 39
liederkreis39.overview: Twelve songs to poems by Joseph von Eichendorff, written in May 1840. There is no story, but one world: forests at night, distant castles, homesickness, moonlight, strange voices and sudden joy. Schumann called it his most romantic music. It moves from loneliness in a foreign land to the rushing happiness of the last song, Frühlingsnacht.

myrthen.title: Myrthen
myrthen.overview: Twenty-six songs to poems by Goethe, Rückert, Heine, Byron, Burns, Mosen and others, which Schumann had bound as a wedding present for Clara in September 1840. Myrtle was the flower of a German bride's wreath. The book opens with Widmung (Dedication) and ends with a second Rückert song, as a frame of love around the whole.

frauenliebe.title: Frauenliebe und -leben
frauenliebe.overview: Eight songs to poems by Adelbert von Chamisso, written in July 1840. A woman tells her life in love: she first sees him, admires him from afar, is chosen, receives his ring, marries, tells him she is expecting a child, holds the child, and loses her husband. The piano's long postlude brings back the music of the first song, as a memory.

gesellen.title: Lieder eines fahrenden Gesellen
gesellen.overview: Songs of a Wayfarer: four songs to Mahler's own words, written in 1884-85 after an unhappy love, and published in 1897. A young journeyman whose sweetheart has married another man walks out into the world: the wedding day, a bright morning in the fields, a knife in his heart, and at last rest under a lime tree. Mahler used music from the second and fourth songs in his First Symphony.

wesendonck.title: Wesendonck-Lieder
wesendonck.overview: Five songs to poems by Mathilde Wesendonck, written in 1857-58 while Wagner, living as a guest of her husband in Zurich, was composing Tristan und Isolde and in love with her. Two of them, Im Treibhaus and Träume, are marked 'study for Tristan und Isolde', and their music passed into the opera.

ariettes.title: Ariettes oubliées
ariettes.overview: 'Forgotten little airs': six songs to poems from Paul Verlaine's Romances sans paroles (1874), written by the young Debussy in 1885-87 and published in 1888; he revised them in 1903 and dedicated the new edition to Mary Garden, his first Mélisande. Rain, wooden horses at a fair, a landscape in Belgium, a gift of fruit and flowers: moods rather than a story.

nuitsdete.title: Les nuits d'été
nuitsdete.overview: Summer Nights: six songs to poems by Théophile Gautier, from his collection La comédie de la mort (1838). Berlioz wrote them for voice and piano in 1840-41 and later scored them for orchestra. From the spring walk of Villanelle through death, absence and a churchyard to the sailor's question in L'île inconnue: 'Where would you like to go, my pretty one?'

shropshire.title: Six Songs from A Shropshire Lad
shropshire.overview: Six poems from A. E. Housman's A Shropshire Lad (1896), set by George Butterworth and published in 1911. Housman's country lads fall in love, play football and go to war, and many die young. Butterworth himself was killed on the Somme in August 1916, at 31, which gives the songs a weight he could not have intended.

tosti-ideale.written: Written and published in 1882 (Ricordi, Milan), dedicated to Jules Devaux
tosti-ideale.story: A man speaks to a woman who is both real and dreamed. He followed her like a rainbow of peace, heard her voice and felt her near, and now, with her gone, begs her to come back to him: with her the bright day would return.
tosti-ideale.poem: Words by Carmelo Errico (1848-1892), a Neapolitan poet and novelist, in Italian.
tosti-ideale.music: One of Tosti's best-loved salon romanze. The melody rises in long, singing arcs over a gentle accompaniment, and the final plea, 'Torna, caro ideal', is the climax: give it the broadest line, not the loudest sound.

schubert-an-die-musik.written: Composed in March 1817 (D 547); published in 1827 as Op. 88 No. 4
schubert-an-die-musik.story: A hymn of thanks to music itself. In grey hours, when life's wild round has caught you, music has lifted the heart into a better world; a sigh from the harp, a sweet chord, has opened heaven. The singer simply says: thank you.
schubert-an-die-musik.poem: Words by Franz von Schober (1796-1882), Schubert's close friend, poet and fellow member of the 'Schubertiade' evenings.
schubert-an-die-musik.music: Two verses to the same music. Listen to the piano's bass line: it moves under the voice like a second melody, almost a duet. The quiet, warm repetition of 'ich danke dir dafür' is the heart of the song.

schubert-standchen.written: Composed in August 1828 (D 957 No. 4); published in 1829 in Schwanengesang
schubert-standchen.story: A serenade sung at night under a window. The lover begs the girl to come down to the quiet grove; the nightingales are pleading for him, the treetops rustle, nobody will betray them. His longing grows until the last 'Komm, beglücke mich!': come, make me happy.
schubert-standchen.poem: Words by Ludwig Rellstab (1799-1860), a Berlin poet and music critic, who had first offered his poems to Beethoven.
schubert-standchen.music: The piano is a guitar or lute plucked under the window, and it answers each of the voice's phrases like an echo. The song is in minor but keeps turning towards major as hope rises.

schubert-heidenroslein.written: Composed on 19 August 1815 (D 257); published in 1821 as Op. 3 No. 3
schubert-heidenroslein.story: A boy sees a little rose on the heath and says he will pick it. The rose answers that she will prick him so he never forgets her. He picks it anyway; she pricks him, but it does no good: she has to suffer it. A folk song on the surface, with a darker story underneath.
schubert-heidenroslein.poem: Words by Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, written in 1771 in the style of a folk song and published in 1789.
schubert-heidenroslein.music: Three short verses to the same tune, as simple as a folk song. Schubert wrote it at 18, on a day he wrote several songs. Keep it light; the story is told by the words, not by drama in the voice.

schubert-die-forelle.written: Composed in 1817 (D 550), revised several times until 1821; first published in 1820
schubert-die-forelle.story: On a clear brook the singer watches a lively trout darting about. A fisherman stands on the bank; as long as the water is clear, the trout is safe. But he grows impatient, stirs up the water, and catches it. The singer watches the betrayed fish with anger.
schubert-die-forelle.poem: Words by Christian Friedrich Daniel Schubart (1739-1791). His poem has a fourth verse, a moral warning young women against seducers, which Schubert left out.
schubert-die-forelle.music: The piano's rippling figure is the bright water and the darting fish. The first two verses share the same music; in the third the music clouds over with the water, then clears again. Schubert later used the melody for the variations of his 'Trout' Quintet (1819).

schubert-du-bist-die-ruh.written: Composed in 1823 (D 776); published in 1826 as Op. 59 No. 3
schubert-du-bist-die-ruh.story: The beloved is peace and longing itself. The singer offers his heart and eyes to her as a dwelling: come in, close the doors behind you, drive out every other pain. The tent of his eyes is lit by her light alone.
schubert-du-bist-die-ruh.poem: Words by Friedrich Rückert (1788-1866), from his collection Östliche Rosen (Eastern Roses, 1822), in the style of Persian poetry.
schubert-du-bist-die-ruh.music: One of the hardest simple songs: slow, quiet and long-breathed. The phrases rise step by step to the climax at 'Dies Augenzelt', which Schubert writes twice. It needs breath control and a steady soft tone more than power.

schubert-ave-maria.written: Composed in 1825 (D 839); published in 1826 as Op. 52 No. 6
schubert-ave-maria.story: Ellen Douglas, hiding in a mountain cave with her exiled father, prays at evening to the Virgin Mary: hear a maiden's prayer, guard us through the night though we are outcasts. It is a prayer for protection, not a church piece: Schubert set it as a song, 'Ellen's third song'.
schubert-ave-maria.poem: From Sir Walter Scott's narrative poem The Lady of the Lake (1810), in Adam Storck's German translation, which is what Schubert set. The Latin 'Ave Maria' words often sung today were fitted to his melody later.
schubert-ave-maria.music: The piano's arpeggios are a harp: in Scott's poem the old minstrel Allan-bane accompanies Ellen. Three verses to the same music; keep the long line floating over the harp.

schubert-gretchen-am-spinnrade.written: Composed on 19 October 1814 (D 118), when Schubert was 17; published in 1821 as Op. 2
schubert-gretchen-am-spinnrade.story: Gretchen sits alone at her spinning wheel. Since she met Faust her peace is gone and her heart is heavy. She pictures him, his walk, his smile, his eyes, his words, and his kiss, and her longing grows until she wishes she could hold him and die of his kisses.
schubert-gretchen-am-spinnrade.poem: From Goethe's Faust, Part One (1808), the scene 'Gretchen's room'. Schubert repeats her first lines as a refrain, and adds them once more at the end.
schubert-gretchen-am-spinnrade.music: The piano is the spinning wheel: the right hand turns, the left hand works the treadle. When she remembers his kiss, the wheel stops; then it starts again, haltingly. The song builds in waves, and each return of 'Meine Ruh ist hin' is a little more desperate.

schubert-der-lindenbaum.written: Composed in February 1827 (D 911 No. 5); published in 1828 in Winterreise
schubert-der-lindenbaum.story: At the town gate stands a lime tree where the wanderer once dreamed sweet dreams and carved words of love. Tonight he passes it in the dark and its branches seem to call him to rest there. A cold wind blows his hat off; he does not turn back. Now, far away, he still hears the rustling: you would find peace here.
schubert-der-lindenbaum.poem: Words by Wilhelm Müller (1794-1827), from his Winterreise poems (1823-24).
schubert-der-lindenbaum.music: The piano's murmuring triplets are the rustling leaves. The memory of the tree is in major and sounds like a folk song; the cold present is in minor, with the wind in the piano. Many people know it as a folk song without knowing it is Schubert's.

schubert-erlkonig.written: Composed in 1815 (D 328), at 18; published in 1821 as Op. 1
schubert-erlkonig.story: A father rides through the night and wind with his sick son in his arms. The boy sees the Erlking, king of the elves, who lures him with games, flowers and his daughters; the father sees only mist, willows and dead leaves. The Erlking takes the boy by force. The father reaches home; in his arms the child is dead.
schubert-erlkonig.poem: A ballad by Goethe, written in 1782 for his play Die Fischerin.
schubert-erlkonig.music: One singer plays four characters: the narrator, the calm father (low), the frightened son (higher, his cry rising each time) and the Erlking (sweet and seductive). The piano's hammering triplets are the galloping horse; they stop for the last line, spoken almost bare: 'war tot'. The right hand's octaves are notoriously tiring for the pianist.

schumann-widmung.written: Composed in 1840 (Op. 25 No. 1); published in 1840 as the first song of Myrthen
schumann-widmung.story: A declaration of love that cannot find enough names for the beloved: my soul, my heart, my joy, my pain, my world, my grave. In the middle it grows calm: you are rest and peace, heaven given to me; your love lifts me above myself.
schumann-widmung.poem: Words by Friedrich Rückert, from his Liebesfrühling (Love's Spring, 1821-1823).
schumann-widmung.music: Schumann's dedication of the whole book to Clara. The outer parts surge; the middle moves to a distant key and quiet, steady chords for 'Du bist die Ruh'. In the last bars the piano quotes the melody of Schubert's Ave Maria.

schumann-im-wunderschonen-monat-mai.written: Composed in May 1840 (Op. 48 No. 1); published in 1844
schumann-im-wunderschonen-monat-mai.story: In the beautiful month of May, when the buds burst, love opened in his heart; when the birds were singing, he told her his longing. Two short verses, and nothing is said of her answer.
schumann-im-wunderschonen-monat-mai.poem: Words by Heinrich Heine, from the Lyrisches Intermezzo in his Buch der Lieder (1827).
schumann-im-wunderschonen-monat-mai.music: The piano begins as if in the middle of a thought and ends on an unresolved chord, as if asking a question. The song never settles in its key, like the poet's hope. Sing it simply, without heaviness: it is only the beginning.

schumann-ich-grolle-nicht.written: Composed in May 1840 (Op. 48 No. 7); published in 1844
schumann-ich-grolle-nicht.story: 'I bear no grudge, even if my heart breaks.' The poet tells his lost love he does not blame her, then says what he saw in a dream: the night in her heart, the snake gnawing at it, how wretched she is. The forgiveness is bitter and not quite true.
schumann-ich-grolle-nicht.poem: Words by Heinrich Heine, from the Lyrisches Intermezzo.
schumann-ich-grolle-nicht.music: Steady, throbbing chords in the piano from the first bar to the last, like a heartbeat that will not calm down. The voice climbs to its climax at the second 'ich grolle nicht'; Schumann prints an optional higher note there for singers who have it.

schumann-mondnacht.written: Composed in May 1840 (Op. 39 No. 5); published in 1842
schumann-mondnacht.story: A moonlit night so still it seems the sky has quietly kissed the earth. A breeze moves over the fields, the woods rustle softly, the night is full of stars. And the soul spreads its wings and flies over the silent land, as if flying home.
schumann-mondnacht.poem: Words by Joseph von Eichendorff, published in 1837.
schumann-mondnacht.music: The piano's soft, high repeated notes are the shimmer of moonlight. The voice sings almost the same phrase again and again, as if holding its breath; only in the last verse, when the soul spreads its wings, does the melody open out.

brahms-wiegenlied.written: Composed in 1868 (Op. 49 No. 4) for the birth of Bertha Faber's second son; published by Simrock in 1868
brahms-wiegenlied.story: Good evening, good night: a mother sings her child to sleep under a cover of roses and carnations. In the second verse angels watch over him and show him the Christmas tree in his dreams.
brahms-wiegenlied.poem: The first verse is from the folk-poem collection Des Knaben Wunderhorn. Brahms added the second verse later, adapted from an 1849 poem by Georg Scherer.
brahms-wiegenlied.music: Brahms wrote it for Bertha Faber, a singer he had known in Hamburg. The piano's gently offbeat accompaniment rocks the cradle and hides an Austrian song she used to sing to him. Keep it simple and warm.

brahms-von-ewiger-liebe.story: At dusk a young man walks his girl home through the dark fields. He says: if you suffer shame because of me, let our love end as quickly as it began. She answers: our love will not end. Iron and steel can be reforged, but our love must last for ever.
brahms-von-ewiger-liebe.poem: Brahms believed the poem was a Wendish (Sorbian) folk text translated by Josef Wenzig; it is in fact by August Heinrich Hoffmann von Fallersleben.
brahms-von-ewiger-liebe.music: A small drama in three parts: a dark, restless opening for the evening walk, the boy's anxious words, and the girl's answer in major and in a new, broader metre that grows to a great climax on 'unsere Liebe muss ewig bestehn'.

brahms-die-mainacht.story: On a May night, under a silver moon, the lonely singer wanders through the bushes. A pair of doves coo to each other; he turns away and looks for darker shade. When will the smiling face that shines like dawn into his soul appear to him? A lonely tear runs down his cheek.
brahms-die-mainacht.poem: Words by Ludwig Hölty (1748-1776), written in 1774. Brahms set three of the poem's four verses.
brahms-die-mainacht.music: Long, slow phrases that need great breath. The middle verse is more agitated and moves to a distant key; the first melody returns for the lonely tear, and the climax, 'die einsame Träne', is the song's peak.

strauss-morgen.written: Composed in May 1894 (Op. 27 No. 4); published in 1894 as a wedding present to Pauline de Ahna
strauss-morgen.story: Tomorrow the sun will shine again, and on the path we take it will unite us, the happy ones. We will go down to the wide shore, look silently into each other's eyes, and the silence of happiness will sink over us.
strauss-morgen.poem: Words by John Henry Mackay (1864-1933), a Scottish-born German poet.
strauss-morgen.music: The piano plays the whole melody first; the voice enters as if joining a thought already begun, and then speaks almost in recitative above it. The last words fall to silence. In Strauss's orchestral version the piano's melody is a solo violin.

faure-apres-un-reve.written: Composed in the 1870s (Op. 7 No. 1); published in 1878
faure-apres-un-reve.story: In a dream the singer saw the beloved: they fled together towards the light, heaven opened its clouds for them. Then the waking: the dream is gone. He begs the night to come back, with its illusions, and give him back the dream.
faure-apres-un-reve.poem: Words by Romain Bussine (1830-1899), a singing teacher at the Paris Conservatoire, freely adapted from an anonymous Italian poem.
faure-apres-un-reve.music: Steady repeated chords in the piano under a long, floating melody that seems to have no place to breathe. The climax comes at the cry 'Reviens, reviens', and then the line sinks back into the night.

faure-lydia.story: The singer praises Lydia's beauty: her rosy cheeks, her white neck, her hair, the morning light of her youth. Forget the dead, he says, let us love; and he ends by giving her his soul in a kiss.
faure-lydia.poem: Words by Charles Leconte de Lisle (1818-1894), the leading poet of the Parnassians, who wrote in the manner of classical Greek and Latin verse.
faure-lydia.music: The melody uses a raised fourth note of the scale, the old Lydian mode, a pun on Lydia's name, which gives it its pure, antique colour. Sing it with an even, unforced line.

debussy-mandoline.written: Composed on 15 November 1882; published in 1890, dedicated to Madame Vasnier
debussy-mandoline.story: The singers of serenades and their lovely listeners exchange idle words under the singing branches: Tircis and Aminte, Clitandre and Damis. Their silk jackets and long trains, their elegance and their blue shadows whirl in the moonlight to the chatter of a mandolin.
debussy-mandoline.poem: Words by Paul Verlaine, from Fêtes galantes (1869), poems inspired by Watteau's paintings of courtly picnics and masked lovers.
debussy-mandoline.music: The piano strums like a mandolin with open fifths. Debussy wrote it at 20 for Marie Vasnier, a singer with a light high soprano. The 'la, la, la' at the end is a little vocalise: keep it light and playful.

hahn-a-chloris.story: A lover tells Chloris that if it is true she loves him, he will never envy even a king's fortune. His happiness is so complete that death could not frighten him: it would only make him lose a little.
hahn-a-chloris.poem: Words by Théophile de Viau (1590-1626), a poet of the early seventeenth century.
hahn-a-chloris.music: Hahn writes in the style of a Baroque air: a slow, walking bass line and a calm, ornamented melody above it, a deliberate homage to Bach. Sing it with a pure, even tone and no romantic swelling.

hahn-l-heure-exquise.written: Composed between 1887 and 1890 as No. 5 of Chansons grises; published in 1891 (Heugel)
hahn-l-heure-exquise.story: The white moon shines in the woods, and from every branch comes a voice under the leaves: O beloved. The pond reflects the silhouette of the willow where the wind is weeping. A vast tenderness seems to come down from the sky. It is the exquisite hour.
hahn-l-heure-exquise.poem: Words by Paul Verlaine, the poem 'La lune blanche' from La bonne chanson (1870).
hahn-l-heure-exquise.music: Hahn wrote it as a teenager. The piano's quiet, rippling figures are the moonlit water. Each verse ends with a hushed refrain; the last, 'C'est l'heure exquise', must be the softest of all.

gounod-serenade.story: A serenade: when you sing, cradled in my arms at evening, do you hear my heart answering? When you laugh, when you sleep, may your dream of me be sweet. A lover's gentle wish over his beloved.
gounod-serenade.poem: Words by Victor Hugo, a serenade from his play Marie Tudor (1833).
gounod-serenade.music: A lilting, swaying song in the style of a barcarolle, with a light, flowing accompaniment. Gounod's melody made it one of the most popular French songs of the century, arranged for every instrument.

massenet-elegie.written: Arranged as a song around 1872; published in 1875 in Massenet's 20 Mélodies
massenet-elegie.story: A lament for the past: sweet spring of other days, green seasons, you have gone for ever. The sky looks dark, the birds no longer sing, the heart is weeping. Without the beloved there is no happy season left.
massenet-elegie.poem: Words by Louis Gallet (1835-1898), a librettist who wrote many of the period's opera texts.
massenet-elegie.music: Massenet's melody began as a piano piece, Mélodie Op. 10 No. 5, and also became the 'Invocation' in his music for Leconte de Lisle's play Les Érinnyes (1873). As a song it was often sung with a cello obbligato. Keep the line legato and the sorrow restrained.

butterworth-loveliest-of-trees.written: Published in 1911 as No. 2 of Six Songs from A Shropshire Lad
butterworth-loveliest-of-trees.story: At Eastertide the cherry tree is hung with white blossom along the woodland ride. The young man counts: he is twenty, and of his seventy years twenty will not come again. Fifty springs are little room to look at things in bloom, so he will go out to see the cherry hung with snow.
butterworth-loveliest-of-trees.poem: Words by A. E. Housman (1859-1936), poem II of A Shropshire Lad (1896).
butterworth-loveliest-of-trees.music: A plain, folk-like melody over quietly moving harmonies; Butterworth collected English folk songs. Butterworth was killed in 1916, at 31; it is hard now to hear the counting of springs without thinking of it.

obradors-del-cabello-mas-sutil.written: Published in 1921 in Canciones clásicas españolas, Vol. 1 (Unión Musical Española, Madrid)
obradors-del-cabello-mas-sutil.story: A lover's song: from the finest hair of your braid I would make a little chain to keep you by my side. I would like to be the water jug in your house, to kiss your mouth when you go to drink.
obradors-del-cabello-mas-sutil.poem: A traditional Spanish popular verse; Obradors called the song one of two 'cantares populares'.
obradors-del-cabello-mas-sutil.music: A slow, intimate melody over a rocking accompaniment. Obradors arranged old and popular Spanish songs in a refined style; this one needs long, warm phrases and a very quiet ending.

schubert-gute-nacht.written: Composed in February 1827 (D 911 No. 1); published in 1828 in Winterreise
schubert-gute-nacht.story: A stranger he came and a stranger he leaves. In May the girl spoke of love, her mother even of marriage; now the world is gloomy and the road is covered in snow. He sets off at night, writes 'good night' on her gate as he passes, so she will see he thought of her.
schubert-gute-nacht.poem: Words by Wilhelm Müller, the opening poem of Winterreise.
schubert-gute-nacht.music: The piano's steady eighth notes are his walking steps, and they never stop. Four verses: the last turns to major as he tiptoes past her door, 'I will not disturb your dreams', then back to minor.

schubert-der-leiermann.written: Composed in autumn 1827 (D 911 No. 24); published in 1828 in Winterreise
schubert-der-leiermann.story: Beyond the village stands an old organ-grinder, turning his hurdy-gurdy with frozen fingers. Barefoot on the ice, his little plate stays empty; nobody listens, dogs growl at him; he lets it all go on. The wanderer asks him: strange old man, shall I go with you? Will you play my songs on your hurdy-gurdy?
schubert-der-leiermann.poem: Words by Wilhelm Müller, the last poem of Winterreise.
schubert-der-leiermann.music: The piano's open fifths in the bass are the drone of the hurdy-gurdy, and a little circling tune repeats in the right hand. The voice is bare and almost still. The cycle ends with a question that is never answered.

schubert-das-wandern.written: Composed in 1823 (D 795 No. 1); published in 1824 in Die schöne Müllerin
schubert-das-wandern.story: Wandering is the miller's joy. He learned it from the water that never rests, from the mill wheels, from the millstones that dance around. O wandering, his delight! Master and mistress, let me go my way in peace.
schubert-das-wandern.poem: Words by Wilhelm Müller, the opening poem of Die schöne Müllerin (1820).
schubert-das-wandern.music: Five verses to the same cheerful tune. The piano's running sixteenth notes are the water and the turning wheel. Sing it fresh and rhythmic, like a young man setting out.

schubert-wohin.written: Composed in 1823 (D 795 No. 2); published in 1824 in Die schöne Müllerin
schubert-wohin.story: The young miller hears a brook rushing from its spring and follows it down the valley, not knowing why. Is this my path? Is it the nymphs singing beneath the water? Let it sing, and follow: there are mill wheels turning in every clear brook.
schubert-wohin.poem: Words by Wilhelm Müller, from Die schöne Müllerin.
schubert-wohin.music: The piano ripples from the first bar to the last: this is the brook that will be the miller's companion through the whole cycle. The voice floats lightly on top, curious and eager.

schubert-auf-dem-wasser-zu-singen.written: Composed in 1823 (D 774); published in 1827 as Op. 72
schubert-auf-dem-wasser-zu-singen.story: In the glow of evening a boat glides over the shimmering waves like a swan. Joy shimmers on the water and in the soul; the red evening light falls on the trees. Time flies away on dewy wings, as it did yesterday and will tomorrow, until I too vanish on its wings.
schubert-auf-dem-wasser-zu-singen.poem: Words by Friedrich Leopold zu Stolberg-Stolberg (1750-1819), written in 1782.
schubert-auf-dem-wasser-zu-singen.music: The piano's falling sixteenth-note figures are the sparkling light on the waves. Each verse begins in minor and turns to major, as the light changes. The vocal line is fast and needs very easy breath and clear words.

schubert-der-musensohn.written: Composed in December 1822 (D 764); published in 1828 as Op. 92 No. 1
schubert-der-musensohn.story: The son of the Muses roams through field and forest, piping his little song; everything moves to his beat. In winter he sings of blossom; young people dance to his tune. But when will he rest in the arms of the one he loves?
schubert-der-musensohn.poem: Words by Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, written in 1799.
schubert-der-musensohn.music: A dancing 6/8 that never stops. The middle verses shift to a brighter key and back. The song needs energy, lightness and very clear German at speed.

schumann-der-nussbaum.written: Composed in 1840 (Op. 25 No. 3); published in 1840 in Myrthen
schumann-der-nussbaum.story: A walnut tree in front of the house spreads its leafy branches. Its blossoms whisper to each other of a girl who dreams day and night of a bridegroom she does not yet know. She listens, smiles, and falls asleep into dreams.
schumann-der-nussbaum.poem: Words by Julius Mosen (1803-1867), a Saxon poet.
schumann-der-nussbaum.music: The piano's rippling figure is the rustling of the leaves, and the voice and piano pass the melody between them as if whispering. The ending, as she drifts into sleep, should be the quietest moment.

schumann-die-lotosblume.written: Composed in 1840 (Op. 25 No. 7); published in 1840 in Myrthen
schumann-die-lotosblume.story: The lotus flower is afraid of the sun's light and waits with bowed head for the night. The moon is her lover; he wakes her with his light, and she opens her face to him. She blooms, glows and trembles with love and love's pain.
schumann-die-lotosblume.poem: Words by Heinrich Heine, from Buch der Lieder (1827).
schumann-die-lotosblume.music: Slow repeated chords in the piano, calm and dense. The song rises gradually to the climax, 'vor Liebe und Liebesweh', and sinks back.

schumann-fruhlingsnacht.written: Composed in May 1840 (Op. 39 No. 12); published in 1842
schumann-fruhlingsnacht.story: Over the garden, through the air, migrating birds pass overhead: spring is coming. Everything begins to bloom. The singer wants to laugh and to weep; it cannot be true. The moon and stars say it, and the nightingales sing it: she is yours!
schumann-fruhlingsnacht.music: The last song of the Liederkreis: the piano's rushing triplet chords never stop, like a heart racing with joy. Breath must be planned carefully, as the voice also hardly pauses.

schumann-waldesgesprach.written: Composed in May 1840 (Op. 39 No. 3); published in 1842
schumann-waldesgesprach.story: A conversation in the forest. A rider meets a beautiful woman riding alone at night and offers to take her home. She warns him: men are deceivers, flee. Then he recognises her: she is the Loreley, the witch of the Rhine. She tells him he will never leave the forest again.
schumann-waldesgesprach.poem: Words by Joseph von Eichendorff, from his novel Ahnung und Gegenwart (1815).
schumann-waldesgesprach.music: The piano's horn calls belong to the rider, a hunting world. The Loreley's answer moves into a different key and a softer colour. The singer plays both: a confident man and a woman who is more than she seems.

schumann-im-rhein-im-heiligen-strome.written: Composed in May 1840 (Op. 48 No. 6); published in 1844
schumann-im-rhein-im-heiligen-strome.story: In the holy river Rhine is reflected the great cathedral of Cologne. In it hangs a painting of the Virgin on golden leather, and her eyes, lips and cheeks are exactly like those of the poet's beloved.
schumann-im-rhein-im-heiligen-strome.poem: Words by Heinrich Heine, from the Lyrisches Intermezzo.
schumann-im-rhein-im-heiligen-strome.music: The piano's heavy dotted rhythms and old-fashioned counterpoint evoke the stone of the cathedral and old church music. The long postlude says what the poet does not: the solemnity is also a little ironic.

schumann-seit-ich-ihn-gesehen.written: Composed in July 1840 (Op. 42 No. 1); published in 1843
schumann-seit-ich-ihn-gesehen.story: Since she first saw him, she thinks she is blind: wherever she looks, she sees only him. His image floats before her as in a waking dream. She no longer wants to play with her sisters; she would rather weep quietly in her room.
schumann-seit-ich-ihn-gesehen.poem: Words by Adelbert von Chamisso (1781-1838), from Frauen-Liebe und Leben (1830).
schumann-seit-ich-ihn-gesehen.music: Slow, hushed chords like a dream. The voice moves calmly within a small range. This music returns at the very end of the cycle, in the piano's postlude, as a memory.

schumann-du-ring-an-meinem-finger.written: Composed in July 1840 (Op. 42 No. 4); published in 1843
schumann-du-ring-an-meinem-finger.story: She speaks to the golden ring on her finger and presses it devoutly to her lips. She had dreamed the peaceful dream of childhood and was lost; the ring has taught her life's true worth. She will serve him and live for him alone.
schumann-du-ring-an-meinem-finger.music: A warm, tender song in which the opening melody returns between the verses like a refrain, as she keeps coming back to the ring. Keep the line steady and intimate.

wolf-verborgenheit.story: 'Leave me, world, leave me be!' The singer does not want to be tempted by gifts of love; let this heart have its own joy and its own pain. He does not know why he weeps; through the tears he sees the light of the sun. Joy flashes through the heaviness in his breast.
wolf-verborgenheit.poem: Words by Eduard Mörike (1804-1875), written in 1832.
wolf-verborgenheit.music: The quiet plea of the outer verses frames a middle section where the music swells with unexplained joy and pain to a powerful climax. One of Wolf's most often sung songs.

wolf-verschwiegene-liebe.story: Over the treetops and the corn, his thoughts fly out into the night: who could guess them? Thoughts are free. If only she could guess who is thinking of her, while the forests rustle; nobody but the night knows it. Secret love.
wolf-verschwiegene-liebe.music: A gently flowing 12/8, quiet throughout, with the harmony changing key often, like thoughts drifting. Wolf marks it softly; the whole song is a whisper.

strauss-cacilie.written: Composed on 9 September 1894 (Op. 27 No. 2), the day before Strauss's wedding to Pauline de Ahna
strauss-cacilie.story: 'If you knew what it is to dream of burning kisses, of wandering and resting with the beloved... if you knew, you would come to me.' Each verse ends with the same urgent wish: if you knew, you would live with me.
strauss-cacilie.poem: Words by Heinrich Hart (1855-1906), a Berlin critic and poet.
strauss-cacilie.music: Ecstatic and fast, with surging arpeggios in the piano. It needs full voice and great stamina; the climax on the last 'du lebtest mit mir!' is one of the high points of Strauss's songs.

mahler-ging-heut-morgen-ubers-feld.written: Composed in 1884-85 (Lieder eines fahrenden Gesellen No. 2); published in 1897
mahler-ging-heut-morgen-ubers-feld.story: He walked across the field this morning: dew on the grass, a finch calling 'Good morning, isn't the world beautiful?', bluebells ringing, the sun making everything sparkle. Will my happiness begin now too? No, no: what I mean, it can never bloom for me.
mahler-ging-heut-morgen-ubers-feld.poem: Words by Gustav Mahler, written after an unhappy love affair in Kassel.
mahler-ging-heut-morgen-ubers-feld.music: A bright, walking melody, the one Mahler used to begin the first movement of his First Symphony. Each verse grows more radiant, until the last lines, where the happiness drains away and the song ends quietly.

wagner-traume.written: Composed in December 1857 (Wesendonck-Lieder No. 5); published in 1862
wagner-traume.story: What wonderful dreams hold my mind: dreams that grow, bloom and fade each day, and leave a scent in the heart, then sink into the grave.
wagner-traume.music: Marked 'study for Tristan und Isolde': its harmonies and its melody return in the love duet of Act 2. Wagner arranged it for violin and small orchestra and had it played under Mathilde's window for her birthday.

clara-schumann-liebst-du-um-schonheit.written: Composed in 1841; published in 1841 as Op. 12 No. 2, in a joint set with Robert Schumann's Op. 37
clara-schumann-liebst-du-um-schonheit.story: If you love for beauty, do not love me: love the sun with its golden hair. If you love for youth, love the spring; for treasure, love the mermaid with her pearls. If you love for love, then love me: I will love you always.
clara-schumann-liebst-du-um-schonheit.poem: Words by Friedrich Rückert, from Liebesfrühling. Clara and Robert published their settings of Rückert poems together, a year after their marriage.
clara-schumann-liebst-du-um-schonheit.music: A light, graceful song with a warm turn at the last verse. Gustav Mahler set the same poem in 1902.

faure-les-roses-d-ispahan.story: The roses of Ispahan in their mossy sheath, the jasmine of Mosul, the orange blossom: none is as sweet as the breath of young Leïlah. But her heart has turned away; let the light, the songs and the roses return with her love.
faure-les-roses-d-ispahan.poem: Words by Charles Leconte de Lisle, in his exotic, oriental manner (published in 1884).
faure-les-roses-d-ispahan.music: A flowing, perfumed accompaniment and a melody that moves in long, supple phrases. The harmony shifts in subtle ways that make the scent and the sadness hard to separate.

faure-mandoline.written: Composed in 1891 in Venice (Op. 58 No. 1, Cinq mélodies 'de Venise'); published in 1891
faure-mandoline.story: The same Verlaine poem Debussy set: serenaders and their ladies exchange idle words under the branches, in silk and lace, whirling in the moonlight to the chatter of a mandolin.
faure-mandoline.poem: Words by Paul Verlaine, from Fêtes galantes (1869).
faure-mandoline.music: Fauré wrote the set while staying in Venice. The piano's crisp chords are the mandolin; the voice is elegant and detached. Compare it with Debussy's setting of the same poem.

debussy-c-est-l-extase-langoureuse.written: Composed in 1885-87 (Ariettes oubliées No. 1); published in 1888, revised in 1903
debussy-c-est-l-extase-langoureuse.story: It is languorous ecstasy, amorous tiredness, the shiver of the woods in the wind, the chorus of small voices in the grey branches. This plaintive soul, mine and yours, breathes out its humble song in the warm evening.
debussy-c-est-l-extase-langoureuse.poem: Words by Paul Verlaine, from Romances sans paroles (1874).
debussy-c-est-l-extase-langoureuse.music: Shimmering, sensual harmonies in the piano and a voice that murmurs more than sings. Debussy uses colour and stillness rather than a clear tune.

debussy-il-pleure-dans-mon-c-ur.written: Composed in 1885-87 (Ariettes oubliées No. 2); published in 1888, revised in 1903
debussy-il-pleure-dans-mon-c-ur.story: It weeps in my heart as it rains on the town. What is this languor that pierces my heart? There is no reason for this grief: neither love nor hate, and that is the worst pain of all, not to know why.
debussy-il-pleure-dans-mon-c-ur.poem: Words by Paul Verlaine, from Romances sans paroles (1874), with an epigraph from Rimbaud: 'It is raining softly on the town.'
debussy-il-pleure-dans-mon-c-ur.music: The piano's constant, falling figures are the rain. In the middle, without a key signature, the music becomes almost bare as the singer searches for a reason.

debussy-green.written: Composed in 1885-87 (Ariettes oubliées No. 5); published in 1888, revised in 1903
debussy-green.story: Here are fruits, flowers, leaves and branches, and here is my heart, which beats only for you. He arrives covered with dew from the morning, and asks to rest at her feet and sleep a little while she rests.
debussy-green.poem: Words by Paul Verlaine, from the 'Aquarelles' (Watercolours) of Romances sans paroles (1874). The English title is Verlaine's.
debussy-green.music: Breathless and eager: the piano's rushing figures and the voice's quick phrases show the lover arriving out of breath. The end slows to rest.

berlioz-villanelle.written: Composed in 1840-41 (Les nuits d'été No. 1); published in 1841, later orchestrated
berlioz-villanelle.story: When the new season comes and the cold has gone, the lovers will go to the woods together to pick lilies of the valley and wild strawberries. They will listen to the blackbirds, talk of love, and come home with baskets full of strawberries.
berlioz-villanelle.poem: Words by Théophile Gautier (1811-1872), from La comédie de la mort (1838).
berlioz-villanelle.music: Three verses to light, staccato chords that skip like footsteps through the woods. Each verse varies the accompaniment a little. Keep it bright, playful and young.

berlioz-absence.written: Composed in 1840-41 (Les nuits d'été No. 4); published in 1841, orchestrated in 1843
berlioz-absence.story: 'Come back, my beloved!' Like a flower far from the sun, the flower of his life is closed far from her. Between them so much distance, so many fields, towns and villages. The refrain returns each time with more longing.
berlioz-absence.poem: Words by Théophile Gautier, from La comédie de la mort (1838).
berlioz-absence.music: The refrain 'Reviens, reviens' is slow, high and held, and it needs great control of soft singing. Berlioz orchestrated this song first, for a singer to perform in concert.

chausson-le-colibri.story: The green hummingbird, king of the hills, flies to a rose and drinks from it so much love that it dies, not knowing whether it could drink it all up. So on the lips of the beloved, the singer would like to die of the first kiss.
chausson-le-colibri.poem: Words by Charles Leconte de Lisle.
chausson-le-colibri.music: Written in 5/4, an unusual metre that gives the song its floating, uneven rhythm, like the darting bird. The melody is long-breathed and the harmonies rich; the ending dies away.
